html:
The first modern wave of Jewish immigration to Ottoman Palestine, from 1882 to 1903. About 25,000 to 35,000 Jews came, most from the Russian Empire after the pogroms that followed the murder of Tsar Alexander II in 1881, and a smaller group from Yemen.

Aliyah is Hebrew for "going up". Many of the newcomers belonged to the Lovers of Zion societies or the student Bilu movement. They founded farming villages such as Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov and Rosh Pinna. Short of money and farming skill, many villages survived only with the backing of Baron Edmond de Rothschild, who paid for vineyards and other crops.

The movement came before political Zionism took shape under Theodor Herzl in the late 1890s. The Second Aliyah from 1904 brought the socialist pioneers who started the kibbutz. Together they laid the ground for the Jewish community of Mandatory Palestine and later the state of Israel, and for its long conflict with the Arabs of Palestine.
